intro: A 167-year-old math problem may have finally fallen — twice in one week. An Anthropic mathematician announced a Lean-verified proof of the Riemann hypothesis developed with substantial help from Claude, while a Stanford postdoc independently produced a purely human-written proof of the even broader General Riemann hypothesis. That headline alone would make for a landmark day, but we've also got a sobering exposé on millions of leaked secrets in the AI supply chain, collapsed UN talks on autonomous weapons, and the question of whether you can repossess a chip floating in orbit.

stories.title: Mathematician at Anthropic claims AI-assisted proof of the Riemann hypothesis
stories.summary: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician employed by Anthropic, announced a Lean-compilable proof of the Riemann hypothesis developed with significant assistance from Claude. The proof uses advanced techniques involving Galois representations, automorphic forms, and cohomology bounds. Several mathematicians, including MIT's Andrew Sutherland, have confirmed the Lean code compiles, though full human understanding will take time. Alpöge timed the announcement after Anthropic's IPO on November 19, 2026. Separately, Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo produced a purely human-written proof of the General Riemann hypothesis, announced by Stanford professor Ravi Vakil. The Riemann hypothesis, dating to 1859, is one of the Millennium Prize problems.
stories.opinion: If either proof withstands scrutiny, this is a landmark moment in mathematics. That the AI-assisted version arrived with formal Lean verification while full human comprehension lags behind is a striking inversion — machines may now prove things faster than humans can understand them. The simultaneous human proof adds a dramatic counterpoint. Where coverage differs: TechCrunch reports the Lean code has been confirmed to compile by several mathematicians including MIT's Andrew Sutherland; The Verge says the proof has not yet been independently verified.

stories.title: Researcher plants 2 million canary secrets into AI supply chain, exposes widespread privacy failures
stories.summary: Security researcher HD Moore planted 2 million unique trackable 'canary' secrets — AWS keys, SSH passwords, unique URLs, DNS names, and git references — into AI prompts sent through the inference supply chain of routers, gateways, and resellers like OpenRouter and Vercel. At least three AI hosting providers were found compromised by attackers siphoning prompts and reusing credentials; multiple resellers logged prompts and passed data to unauthorized parties; and multiple providers ignored Zero Data Retention privacy flags.
stories.opinion: This is the most concrete evidence yet that the sprawling AI inference middleman ecosystem is a serious security liability. Organizations sending sensitive data through third-party AI pipelines should treat every hop as a potential leak point.

stories.title: International talks on controlling autonomous weapons collapse after Russian objections
stories.summary: Week-long negotiations at the UN Review Conference on Conventional Weapons in Geneva failed to establish a mandate for a legally binding treaty on autonomous weapons, collapsing early Saturday morning after Russia's objections could not be overcome despite overwhelming majority support from other states.
stories.opinion: The collapse leaves lethal autonomous weapons development in a regulatory vacuum at exactly the moment the underlying AI capabilities are accelerating. Without a treaty framework, norms will be set by whichever militaries deploy first.

stories.title: METR's updated AI benchmark reveals growing gap between verifiable and open-ended reasoning
stories.summary: AI evaluation nonprofit METR released an updated 'time horizon plot' measuring AI capability by the length of human-calibrated tasks models can complete. While AI continues improving exponentially on verifiable tasks like coding and math, it lags significantly on tasks requiring judgment and open-ended reasoning. No AI-designed evaluation was deemed useful by METR researchers, despite frontier models surpassing most humans at software engineering.
stories.opinion: The update usefully punctures the narrative that AI progress is uniform across all cognitive tasks. The distinction between verifiable and judgment-heavy work has major implications for which jobs and workflows AI will actually transform near-term.

stories.title: Spotify founder Daniel Ek backs AI researcher's fusion power startup Europa Fusion
stories.summary: Daniel Ek is backing Europa Fusion, a UK-based fusion startup founded in February by Nantas Nardelli, an AI researcher with experience at DeepMind, Facebook AI Research, and Microsoft Research. Nardelli left Pacific Fusion over disagreements about approach, believing fusion startups should invest more in simulation and data-driven methods. Europa Fusion will pursue a pulsed-power approach using massive, precisely timed electrical surges to compress fuel targets.
stories.opinion: Nardelli's bet that AI-driven simulation can shortcut fusion engineering is a novel thesis, but it's unproven and the pulsed-power approach remains one of the least mature fusion pathways.

stories.title: Chess.com launches classic games hub with backgammon, go, mahjong, and more
stories.summary: Chess.com is expanding beyond chess with a Classic Games platform in public beta, adding 10 games including backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative. The company, with nearly 300 million members, says AI helped enable the expansion. The platform will be available on web, iOS, and Android.
stories.opinion: Chess.com's massive community is a genuine distribution advantage for classic games that lack comparable online hubs. Whether chess players convert to backgammon or go enthusiasts remains the open question.

stories.title: CoreWeave's mounting debt raises questions about AI infrastructure boom sustainability
stories.summary: An analysis profiles CoreWeave as the 'poster child of the AI bubble,' highlighting the increasingly risky, debt-laden business model behind massive datacenter buildouts. The piece draws parallels to historical infrastructure projects, notes local opposition to datacenter development, and questions whether AI will deliver sufficient returns to justify the enormous capital expenditure.
stories.opinion: CoreWeave is the clearest stress test of whether the AI infrastructure buildout will pay off or become this cycle's overbuilt fiber-optic network. The company's debt load makes it the canary in the coal mine for AI capex sustainability.

stories.title: Trump threatens 'tremendous tax' on companies building AI data centers outside the US
stories.summary: President Trump threatened to impose a tax on companies building AI data centers abroad, warning that China would otherwise capture the market. He made the remarks at a press conference following a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Putin. The proposal appeared off-the-cuff, with Trump admitting he hadn't discussed it with his own staff. Implementation could face challenges from an incoming Democratic congressional majority, and the threat comes amid growing domestic restrictions on data center construction across US states and cities.
stories.opinion: The threat highlights a genuine tension: the US wants to keep AI infrastructure domestic but is simultaneously making it harder to build domestically through local restrictions. An off-the-cuff tax proposal is unlikely to resolve that contradiction.

stories.title: Engineers race to build robotic hands that match human dexterity
stories.summary: Human hand dexterity remains one of the last major barriers preventing AI and robots from fully replacing human labor. Engineers and robotics experts are racing to develop robotic hands matching the anatomical complexity of human hands, with Amazon warehouses serving as a key example where current robots struggle with varied manipulation tasks.
stories.opinion: Hand dexterity is indeed the bottleneck, but the article's framing as the last barrier to making humanity 'obsolete' oversells the timeline. Even with better hands, the integration of perception, planning, and manipulation in unstructured environments remains formidable.

stories.title: Space data centers face unique financing hurdle: chips in orbit can't be repossessed
stories.summary: Lenders typically use chips as collateral for data center loans, but chips launched into orbit cannot be repossessed. Lenders behind SpaceX's $40 billion chip financing deal requested no purchased chips be used for orbital data centers. Elon Musk claims space will be the cheapest place for data centers within two to three years, contingent on reusable Starship flights. Google may hold an advantage deploying its own TPU chips in space through Project Suncatcher.
stories.opinion: The collateral problem is a genuinely novel financial constraint that could slow space data center development regardless of technical feasibility. Self-funded players like Google have a structural edge here over debt-dependent competitors.

tweet_headlines.author: shannholmberg
tweet_headlines.headline: Shannon Holmberg's 2027 AI marketing predictions: __PR makes a comeback via AI search citations__, and brands shift to fewer, longer creator partnerships.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
AI marketing predictions for 2027 (use this list to get ahead)

1. PR comes back

AI search chats (ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude etc.) recommend the brands that many sites write about

> an agent finds publications and podcasts where you can pitch yourself as a thought leader
> another agent asks these AI search chats your customers' questions every week and records which brands they recommend

2. brands sign fewer, longer creator partnerships

one-off sponsored posts get less trust

> an agent lists the creators your customers follow and checks if their audience fits
> it drafts the outreach, then you run campaigns in waves, since customers need several touchpoints before they trust you

3. power users get harder to reach

more products launch, and they all compete for the same early users

4. employee-led content brings in more growth

buyers trust people more than brand accounts

5. more video, filmed raw by real people

as more content gets made with AI, raw videos from real people stand out

> an agent finds trends and customer pain points for your next video
> you film it yourself
> AI edits it and handles ops like scheduling

6. more companies open-source their tools

a free, open-source tool introduces people to the problem your paid product solves

as software gets easier to replicate, your edge is no longer the product itself but how many users you can get interested, and most of them will never host themselves = your solution wins in the long run

7. companies buy distribution

Stan, the company behind the AI content assistant Stanley, bought Typefully and its nearly 10,000 paying customers in November

8. more ads in AI search chats

ChatGPT already shows ads, more AI labs will follow

tweet_headlines.author: asmartbear
tweet_headlines.headline: WP Engine founder Jason Cohen argues the __10x markup over GoDaddy__ earns its keep — customers include global banks, hacked small businesses, and fast-food chains running multilingual campaigns.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
WP Engine charged $50 a month to host WordPress. GoDaddy charged $5.

That's 10 times the price, for the same open-source software. Who pays that?

It's not just "big businesses" or "small businesses".

• Small businesses that had been hacked and never wanted to go through that again.
• One of the largest banks in the world, so its branches could publish their own content.
• One of the largest software companies in the world, for its developer-relations portal.
• One of the largest fast-food chains in the world, so local agencies in small countries could publish social content and get the language and culture right.
• News sites that could get 100 times their normal traffic the day a big story broke.

A global bank, a media site, and a small business that got hacked have nothing in common using typical demographics.

But they all valued the same thing: enterprise-grade quality with the flexibility of open source, at a price between cheap hosting and an enterprise CMS. That was our target market.

To a small business, we were the best option. To an enterprise, we were the cheap alternative.

https://t.co/gW8zLV1eAb

tweet_headlines.source_text:
We went from 140 people to 20 at AppSumo. 

These are the 6 company rules:

🤖 Zero-person work. Be the last person to do it by hand.

💻 Everyone ships. Bring copy we can send, a page we can launch, or a prototype. Not ideas.

💰 Everyone profitable. Every project pays for itself.

🎯 Own outcomes. Don't wait to be told what to do.

🙅 No meetings. Write it down, decide, ship. 

⚡ Make fast faster. Ask why great takes this long. Then fix it.
